title: Firstfruits, the Poor's Tithe, and a Covenant Declared
summary: Moses gives two ceremonies for Israel's life in the land. At the harvest each worshiper brings a basket of firstfruits to the sanctuary and recites Israel's story from a wandering Aramean to the gift of the land, then rejoices with the Levite and the foreigner. In the third year the tithe goes to the Levite, foreigner, fatherless, and widow, with a declaration of obedience and a prayer for blessing. The chapter ends with the covenant stated from both sides: Israel declares that the LORD is its God, and the LORD declares Israel his treasured people.
story: This chapter closes the long law code that began in chapter 12. Having set out how Israel is to live in the land, Moses now describes what they will say and do once they are there. The worshiper's words compress the whole story of Genesis and Exodus into a few sentences: the patriarchs, the descent into Egypt, slavery, the cry to God, the exodus, and the gift of the land. The chapter's final verses (16-19) form a hinge between the laws and the blessings and curses of chapters 27 and 28, stating the covenant relationship in formal terms. Israel is about to cross the Jordan, and the chapter imagines the day when the promises will be tasted in the first harvest of the land.
historical:
The ceremonies assume Israel settled in Canaan and worshiping at the place the LORD will choose, the central sanctuary Deuteronomy anticipates (later Shiloh and eventually Jerusalem). The confession of verses 5-9 has attracted much scholarly attention. The German Old Testament scholar Gerhard von Rad argued in the 1930s that it was an ancient creed, one of the oldest summaries of Israel's faith, around which the larger story of the Pentateuch grew. Many later scholars questioned how early the passage is, but its character as a compact confession of faith is widely recognized.

The wandering Aramean of verse 5 is most often identified with Jacob, whose mother Rebekah came from Aram, who lived for twenty years in Aram with Laban, and who went down to Egypt with his family. Some interpreters think Abraham is meant, since he too came from the region of Aram. The Hebrew word translated wandering can also mean perishing or ready to perish, and the Greek and Aramaic translations and later Jewish tradition read the verse in different ways. Either sense fits Jacob, a homeless and threatened man whose descendants became a great nation.
cultural:
The firstfruits were the first ripe produce of the harvest, brought to God before the rest was used. The offering acknowledged that the land and its produce were God's gift, and it was accompanied by a spoken confession, a reminder that worship in Israel involved telling the story as well as giving gifts. The Mishnah, compiled around AD 200, has a whole tractate (Bikkurim) describing how firstfruits were later brought to the temple in Jerusalem in procession.

The third-year tithe (described already in 14:28-29) was stored in the local towns and given to those without land or family support. The worshiper's declaration in verse 14 disavows practices associated with mourning and the cult of the dead, which were common in the ancient Near East, where food offerings were placed for deceased ancestors. Israel's gifts were for the living poor, not the dead. The phrase a land flowing with milk and honey described the pastoral and agricultural richness of the land, milk from flocks and honey (possibly date syrup as well as bee honey) from its produce.
literary: The chapter is built around three spoken declarations, each introduced by instructions for what the worshiper does. In verses 3 and 5-10 the worshiper speaks at the altar, moving from third person (my father) to first person plural (us, we) and finally to first person singular (I have brought), so that each generation places itself inside the exodus story. In verses 13-15 the worshiper speaks a statement of faithfulness followed by a prayer. Verses 17-19 use a formal pair of today statements, you have proclaimed and the LORD has proclaimed, mirroring each other the way the two parties to a covenant would declare their commitments.

outline.t: The basket of firstfruits brought to the priest
The confession: from a wandering Aramean to the land
The third-year tithe and the prayer for blessing
The covenant declared by both parties

doctrines.note: Verses 16-19 state the covenant as a mutual declaration: Israel proclaims that the LORD is its God, and the LORD proclaims Israel his treasured possession. The relationship is personal and binding on both sides.

The confession tells salvation as history: God heard, saw, brought out, brought in, and gave. Israel's worship begins not with what the worshiper has achieved but with what God has done for a people who cried to him from slavery.

Worship and care for the poor belong together. The same chapter that brings firstfruits to the altar sends the tithe to the Levite, the foreigner, the fatherless, and the widow, and it calls them to rejoice together.

words.note: Reshit, first or beginning. It is the word that opens Genesis (in the beginning), and here it means the first and best of the harvest. Giving the reshit to God declared that the whole harvest came from him and belonged to him.

Arammi, Aramean. Aram was the region of northern Mesopotamia and Syria where Abraham's relatives settled. Calling Israel's ancestor an Aramean was a humble confession: the nation began not as natives of the land but as outsiders and migrants.

Ma'aser, tithe, a tenth. Deuteronomy's tithe laws direct it partly to celebratory meals at the sanctuary and, every third year, to the local poor. Here the worshiper calls it the sacred portion and declares that he has given it away as commanded.

Segullah, treasured possession. The word describes a king's personal treasure, set apart from general property. God first used it of Israel at Sinai (Exodus 19:5), and Peter applies the idea to the church as a people for God's own possession (1 Peter 2:9).

christ: Paul calls the risen Christ the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep (1 Corinthians 15:20). The image comes from offerings like the one in this chapter: the first sheaf or basket presented to God is the pledge that the whole harvest will follow. Christ's resurrection is the first part of a harvest in which his people will also be raised. The chapter's confession also has a pattern that the gospel repeats. Israel's worshiper told how God heard a cry, brought a people out of slavery, and gave them an inheritance, and the New Testament tells how God in Christ redeemed a people from sin and death and gave them an inheritance that cannot perish (1 Peter 1:3-4). The language of a treasured possession and a holy people is carried directly into the church's identity (1 Peter 2:9; Titus 2:14). These are connections the New Testament itself draws, not allegories read into the ceremony.

hard.q: Isn't it self-righteous for the worshiper to declare, I have done everything You commanded me?
hard.a:
Verse 14 can sound like a boast, especially to readers shaped by the New Testament's warnings against self-righteousness. In context, however, the declaration is narrow and specific. The worshiper is affirming that he has handled the tithe faithfully: he has given it to the poor, not eaten it in mourning, not used it while unclean, and not offered it to the dead. It is the kind of statement an honest steward makes about a particular task, not a claim to sinless perfection.

The declaration also comes after a confession that everything Israel has is God's gift (verses 5-10), and it ends in a prayer, not a demand: look down and bless your people. Readers across traditions have noted that Old Testament faith regularly joins humble dependence on God's grace with sincere, specific obedience. The Psalms contain similar statements of integrity (Psalm 26, for example). The danger Jesus later exposes, in the Pharisee who thanked God he was not like others (Luke 18:11-12), is obedience turned into contempt for others, which is the opposite of this chapter's generosity.

questions: The worshiper told Israel's story as his own, moving from my father to us to I. Whose story of God's faithfulness do you need to learn to tell as your own?
The firstfruits were given before the rest of the harvest was used. What would it look like to give God the first and not the leftovers?
The same chapter joins worship at the altar with food for the widow and the stranger. How closely are worship and generosity joined in your life?
